issues.subcategory: non-representative full sample / overclaim of representativeness
issues.description: The total analytic sample of 4,000 is not nationally representative because 1,500 participants are a targeted oversample of past-year sports bettors. For all non-gambling outcomes (pornography, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription/illicit drugs), pooling this oversample with the 2,500-person representative panel biases prevalence and associations in unknown ways, yet the manuscript repeatedly characterizes the whole study as 'nationally representative.' No weighting scheme is proposed to recover representativeness.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500).

issues.subcategory: gambling sample dominated by sports bettors
issues.description: Because 100% of the 1,500-person oversample are gamblers and they are pooled with the representative panel, the gambling analyses (effective N=3,325) are heavily weighted toward sports bettors. Conclusions about whether moral incongruence predicts gambling problems will therefore not generalize to gamblers in general, undermining the headline comparison with pornography.
issues.quote: Gambling | 73%  (national sample) 100%  (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: measurement of tobacco vs. non-tobacco nicotine contradicts analysis plan
issues.description: Frequency and moral disapproval are measured with a single combined 'tobacco/nicotine' item, but the analysis plan specifies computing a separate problematic-use composite for 'tobacco' and 'non-tobacco nicotine' as distinct substances. It is impossible to estimate separate frequency-by-disapproval interactions for two substances that were assessed with one combined frequency and one combined disapproval item. Table 2 also lists only a single 'Tobacco/Nicotine' row.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: inconsistent count of outcomes and analyses
issues.description: The manuscript variously refers to 'eight proposed outcomes,' '8 target behaviors/variables,' and '10 moderation analyses.' Enumerating the described DVs (alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, cannabis, prescription, illicit, plus pornography and gambling each on two measures) does not reconcile cleanly with these figures, leaving the actual number of confirmatory tests ambiguous.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: altered scoring of validated instrument (PGSI)
issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index is a validated instrument with response options scored 0-1-2-3 and a summed total with established clinical cutoffs. The supplemental materials show non-standard anchors scored Never(0), Sometimes(2), Most of the time(4), Almost Always(5), and the text states responses will be averaged rather than summed. This invalidates the instrument's norms and severity interpretation.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale described differently in text vs. supplement
issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen is described in the main text as a three-point scale from 0 (never) to 2 (very often), but the supplemental table shows the anchors coded 0 (never), 2 (occasionally), 4 (very often). These are different scorings of the same instrument, and the supplemental coding departs from the validated 0–2 scoring.
issues.quote: on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: outcome measures capture objective harm, not 'self-reported feelings of addiction'
issues.description: The theoretical claim is that moral incongruence inflates subjective feelings of addiction (potential false positives), which requires DVs that are purely perceptual. However, the PGSI and ASSIST consequence items assess actual harms (financial problems, health problems, failure to meet obligations, others' concern). If incongruence predicts these, it could reflect real consequences rather than misperception, confounding the interpretation that incongruence produces spurious addiction reports.
issues.quote: how often has your use of or engagement in the following led to health, social, legal, or financial problems for you?

issues.subcategory: restricted moderator variance / null-by-design among users
issues.description: Moral-disapproval items will only be analyzed among people who engage in each behavior. People who strongly morally disapprove of a behavior (e.g., illicit drugs, alcohol) are less likely to engage in it, so among users the disapproval moderator will have a restricted, possibly floor-bound range. This selection could produce the predicted null interactions for substances/gambling for purely psychometric reasons (range restriction), not because moral incongruence is genuinely absent—directly threatening the central equivalence-test inference.
issues.quote: That is, we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.

issues.subcategory: social-desirability bias correlated with the moderator
issues.description: Self-reported frequency of stigmatized behaviors (illicit drug use, pornography use) is subject to underreporting that is plausibly stronger among moral disapprovers. Because moral disapproval is also the moderator, this systematic, moderator-correlated measurement error could attenuate or distort the frequency-by-disapproval interaction differentially across behaviors, biasing the comparison the study hinges on. No validity checks or bias-correction are proposed.
issues.quote: we will assess past year frequency of alcohol use, nicotine products, prescription drugs for non-medical reasons, and illegal drugs.

issues.subcategory: use of unvalidated common-scale items for pornography and gambling
issues.description: Placing pornography and gambling within the NIDA-ASSIST 'for fully parallel analysis' uses these items in an unvalidated way and then includes them as outcomes (Table 1 lists 'modified NIDA-ASSIST items' as a pornography/gambling measure). The bare assertion that this 'will not decrement our ability' is not supported by psychometric evidence, and parallelism does not guarantee construct equivalence across substances and behaviors.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval—the key moderator—is operationalized with a single item per behavior, precluding reliability estimation and likely attenuating interaction effects unevenly across behaviors. Single-item moderators with measurement error are especially problematic for detecting interactions, which are already low-power and attenuated by unreliability.
issues.quote: we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: operationalization mismatch with the diagnostic caveat being tested
issues.description: The ICD-11 CSBD caveat concerns moral distress/disapproval per se (closer to a 'direct effect'), yet the study predicts that the direct effect of moral disapproval on problems is significant and NON-unique (present for substances and gambling too). The claimed uniqueness rests only on the interaction term. Thus even if hypotheses are confirmed, the result shows morality's direct contribution is universal, which does not straightforwardly support the framing that the CSBD moral-distress caveat is uniquely warranted for sexual behavior.
issues.quote: Specifically, we do expect moral disapproval of substances among substance users to positively predict self-reported problems, even when including use frequency, religiousness, gender, and age as covariates in a regression model.

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from pornography to 'sexual behavior'/CSBD
issues.description: The study measures only pornography use but repeatedly frames conclusions as bearing on 'sexual behavior,' 'compulsive sexual behaviors,' and the CSBD diagnosis, which encompasses many behaviors beyond pornography. Demonstrating a pornography-specific interaction cannot establish that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior broadly or validate the CSBD caveat.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: SESOI derived from a different construct than tested
issues.description: The equivalence region (δ=.11) is anchored to an interaction between religiousness and use, whereas the confirmatory tests use moral disapproval × frequency. The authors acknowledge this mismatch but still adopt the religiousness-based estimate as the benchmark for a moral-disapproval-based effect, making the calibration of the 'smallest effect of interest' conceptually inconsistent with the tested effect.
issues.quote: Notably, this effect was observed for an interaction between religiousness (as opposed to moral disapproval directly) and pornography viewing frequency in predicting self-reported addiction.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous/inconsistent SESOI metric
issues.description: The smallest effect of interest is specified inconsistently: the G*Power analysis targets f2 = .015, while the equivalence region is set to δ = β = .11 with a reported f2 = .016. It is unclear which value defines the SESOI, and the two are not equated, creating ambiguity about the actual threshold for null/equivalence decisions.
issues.quote: the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015)

issues.subcategory: inconsistent reported effect size for same study
issues.description: The effect from Grubbs, Lee, et al. (2020) is reported as Cohen's d = .22 in one place and Cohen's d = .25 in another, for what is described as the same interaction effect. This undermines confidence in the effect-size bookkeeping used to set the equivalence region.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .012,  f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: multicollinearity between covariate and moderator
issues.description: Religiousness is entered as a covariate while moral disapproval is the moderator, yet the manuscript itself states religiousness is the strongest predictor of moral disapproval. High collinearity between religiousness and moral disapproval (and their products with frequency) can destabilize interaction estimates and inflate standard errors, complicating both the significance tests and the equivalence tests.
issues.quote: religiousness still appears to be the best predictor of moral disapproval of pornography

issues.subcategory: implausible assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The plan assumes no unplanned missingness and no need to remove careless responders based on the vendor's proprietary standards. For sensitive self-reports (illicit drug use, pornography), item nonresponse, refusal, and careless responding are likely. No missing-data handling, attention checks, or sensitivity analyses are specified, leaving a key threat unaddressed.
issues.quote: Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: alcohol frequency operationalization mismatched to construct
issues.description: Alcohol 'frequency' will be assessed as any consumption regardless of quantity, discarding the heavy-drinking (4/5+ drinks) information that is more relevant to problematic use. A general consumption-frequency predictor is a weak proxy for the construct (risky/problematic alcohol use), potentially biasing the frequency-by-disapproval interaction for alcohol relative to other behaviors.
issues.quote: for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: undisclosed multiple-comparison control for confirmatory tests
issues.description: Holm correction is specified only for bivariate correlations, but roughly ten moderation models plus their direct-effect and equivalence tests are run without any stated family-wise error control. Given the directional, comparison-based hypotheses across many behaviors, the absence of a correction strategy for the confirmatory tests is a researcher-degrees-of-freedom concern.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: vague, conditional analysis-switching rules
issues.description: The plan to switch from OLS to DWLS latent-variable models is triggered by assumptions being 'substantially violated' and supplemental analyses run 'as appropriate,' without quantitative thresholds. These undefined criteria leave room for outcome-dependent analytic choices in what is intended to be a pre-registered confirmatory study.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: underpowered subgroups invalidate equivalence inference
issues.description: For prescription drug misuse (estimated achieved power .301) and illicit substances (.472–.764), the design is underpowered to detect even the SESOI, so a non-significant or 'equivalent' result cannot license a null/equivalence conclusion. The proposed fallback (re-defining the equivalence region to the lower bound of a larger β=.27 effect) substantially weakens the inference to merely 'smaller than a large pornography effect,' which does not establish practical nullity or true uniqueness.
issues.quote: Prescription Drug Misuse | 3.5% | 140 | .057 | .301

issues.subcategory: inconsistent frequency-scale numbering across instruments
issues.description: Substance frequency is described as a 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) scale, while pornography frequency is described as 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). Using different numeric codings for the same conceptual scale risks errors in centering, interaction construction, and cross-behavior comparison.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: coarse/ambiguous gender operationalization
issues.description: Gender is entered as a binary '1 = male, 0 = not-male,' collapsing women and nonbinary participants and inconsistent with the survey's branching that uses discrete 'MAN'/'WOMAN' categories for the alcohol items. This both loses information and creates an internal inconsistency in how a key covariate is defined.
issues.quote: Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: confirmation-oriented framing of hypotheses
issues.description: The study repeatedly frames its purpose as 'demonstrating' a desired outcome (uniqueness of moral incongruence to sexual behavior) rather than neutrally testing it. This directional, goal-confirming language is in tension with the equivalence-testing logic and raises concern about interpretive bias in a confirmatory report.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: frequency-confounded item within the problem composite
issues.description: The substance 'problematic use' composite averages in a craving-frequency item ('how often have you had a strong desire or urge...') scored on the same 0–5 frequency metric as the predictor. For high-frequency substances (e.g., nicotine), urge frequency is mechanically tied to use frequency, inflating frequency–problem associations independent of any incongruence process and biasing interaction estimates non-uniformly across behaviors.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use (“In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?”

issues.subcategory: incomplete/garbled methods sentence
issues.description: The description of the power analyses contains an incomplete sentence ('a series of estimated achieved power based.'), leaving unclear how achieved power was estimated and on what assumptions, which hampers evaluation and replication of the power planning.
issues.quote: and a series of estimated achieved power based. The results are summarized in Table 2 below.

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional design
issues.description: Although the limitations section acknowledges that the cross-sectional data preclude causal inference, the hypotheses and aims use causal verbs ('influences,' 'amplifies,' 'drives'), which risks readers interpreting moderation findings as evidence that moral incongruence causally produces feelings of addiction.
issues.quote: moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior) influences self-perceived feelings of addiction
